transcript:
Meeting Header:
Date: 2026-05-07 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Alex (Redwood AE), Priya (Redwood SE), Jordan (Veridian SRE), Lina (Veridian CISO), Sam (Veridian Legal), Elliot (Veridian Infra)

[00:00:02] Alex (Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick round of intros, and then we'll go through the governance artifacts you asked about and the DR playbook.
[00:00:12] Jordan (Veridian): Hey, Jordan here. We're mainly focused on SRE runbooks and RTO targets. Lina will drive the security considerations.
[00:00:18] Lina (Veridian): Hi all. Mostly me and Sam for compliance; we want to understand the audit surface and KMS story for private deployments.
[00:00:24] Priya (Redwood): Great, thanks. I'll start with an overview of our private control plane and key encryption controls, then Alex will cover certification artifacts.

--- Summary / quick bullets (auto-gen may be off) ---
- Redwood to provide SOC 2 Type II, controls matrix, and private deployment KMS diagram
- Discussed SSO options: SAML, OIDC, SCIM for provisioning; RBAC model in Console
- Reviewed incident escalation tiers and suggested tabletop schedule

[00:02:10] Priya (Redwood SE): So on the private deployment side, we ship a customer-managed control plane that sits in your VPC, you manage the network and there's an agent that talks back for telemetry. For keys we support CMEK via your KMS provider, and we can integrate with cloud HSM or on-prem HSMs.
[00:02:40] Elliot (Veridian): When you say CMEK, is that cross-region? We need keys to be region-scoped because of residency.
[00:02:47] Priya: Yes, you can scope keys per region. Our deployment templates allow per-region KMS endpoints. We also recommend local key mirrors for cross-region failover, but the primary key can be region-bound to satisfy residency.
[00:03:12] Lina: How do you handle audit logs? We need immutable logs with tamper-evidence and 7 year retention for certain PII flows.
[00:03:22] Priya: Audit logs are configurable. We stream structured audit events to your logging cluster (we support S3, BigQuery, SIEMs). Events include admin actions, model uploads, key rotations, and API token issuance. There is an append-only mode and we can enable object-lock on S3. Note transcription might refer to 'KV cash' but that's actually KV cache events for inference cache.
[00:04:05] Sam (Legal): For legal, we need to see the data flow diagram and proof of encryption in transit and at-rest. Also, we need certificate-chain evidence for TLS and details on who holds the keys.
[00:04:18] Alex: We'll send a redacted data flow diagram and a controls matrix that maps to SOC 2. The Type II report is recent — 2026 Q1 — we'll attach it. On TLS, all endpoints are TLS1.2+; we maintain cert rotation; customers can bring their own certs for the private control plane.

[00:05:40] Priya: On SSO and RBAC, we support SAML2 and OIDC, SCIM for provisioning, and granular roles in the Console. The role model has project-level roles, model-level roles and token scopes. You can restrict token creation to admins only.
[00:06:05] Jordan: We want to avoid people creating long-lived tokens ad-hoc. Can you force short TTLs and MFA for admin actions?
[00:06:12] Priya: Yes, we support token TTL policies and session policies. For admin actions we can enforce SAML with enforced MFA via your IdP. There's also an audit trail per token so you can tie actions back to SAML identities.

[00:07:02] Elliot: Curious about e-discovery: if we need records for a tenancy, how easy is it to pull request-scoped logs?
[00:07:10] Priya: You can export request logs filtered by tenant, model, or time range. We keep request hashes and pointers to stored payloads; raw request payload retention is configurable per customer. For regulated PII you can configure redaction or not store full payloads.

[00:08:30] Lina: Let's turn to incident response and BCDR. Our initial ask: what are typical RTO and RPO for your dedicated clusters, and what's the escalation path if a region goes down?
[00:08:45] Alex: High-level: for hosted, our multi-region fallback is designed for continuity but can't guarantee identical latency. For Dedicated and Private you get SLA-backed nodes and a documented escalation matrix. Typical RTOs depend on workload; we've seen 15 min to re-route for stateless endpoints but for stateful model KV cache warm-up it can be 20-45 minutes.
[00:09:12] Priya: Important nuance: the KV cache and model warm-up drive effective RTO. We use prefix caching and warm-start artifacts — if you use persistent checkpoints and pre-warmed workers, you can get under 10-15 minutes for critical routes. Without warmers it's 30+ minutes.
[00:09:40] Jordan: Those numbers help. Our bar for checkout flows is 5 minutes RTO for core payments flow, which is tough — can Redwood meet that?
[00:09:50] Priya: We'd do a hybrid: keep a small dedicated pool pinned to the checkout model and use autoscale for less-critical models. That pinned pool improves RTO to very low levels, and it's something we can size and quote.
[00:10:16] Elliot: And what's the failover mechanism? Do you do active-active or active-passive?
[00:10:22] Priya: Both are supported. For ultra-low RTO we recommend active-active across zones with traffic steering at the edge. For cost-conscious setups, active-passive with warm standby is typical.

[00:11:08] Sam: On escalation, what are the tiers and contacts? We need an on-call list and SLA burn thresholds that trigger executive escalation.
[00:11:18] Alex: Our standard escalation matrix: Tier 0 automated alerts and runbooks; Tier 1 SE on-call; Tier 2 Infra/Runtime; Tier 3 Eng + Exec. For enterprise we provide a dedicated SE who can be paged and a named SLA lead. We can map thresholds to % error rate, token latency, or throughput drops.
[00:11:46] Lina: Can we get a sample runbook for a region outage showing exact steps, who calls, and expected times?
[00:11:53] Priya: Yes — we'll share a redacted runbook which shows checks (network, KMS, model health), reroute commands, and warm-start instructions. It includes playbook snippets like 'promote warm node', 'invalidate cache prefix', and 'update edge route'.

[00:13:05] Jordan: Two practical questions: 1) When you rotate keys, is there a window where old tokens are invalidated? 2) If the KMS provider is unavailable, do you have a cached decrypt path?
[00:13:14] Priya: Key rotation is orchestrated: we support key versioning and key id in metadata; existing tokens remain valid until they expire or are revoked. For KMS outages, we strongly recommend a key-tiering approach: a short-term key cache (for decrypt) with strict TTL and audit, and a recovery key in a separate HSM region. That does add complexity but reduces dependency.

[00:14:45] Alex: From a compliance perspective, we'll map our controls to SOC 2 Trust Services Criteria and to common ISO 27001 clauses. Lina, Sam — would you prefer the controls matrix in spreadsheet form or a narrative mapping?
[00:14:58] Sam: Spreadsheet is better for legal review, please include control IDs, descriptions, and evidence pointers.
[00:15:08] Alex: Noted. We'll include evidence pointers such as logs, config snapshots, and the audit trail for key ops.

[00:18:30] Priya: Quick note on observability: we expose per-token cost and latency breakdowns; for DR exercises we can stream detailed traces to your tracing backend to help with root cause.
[00:18:44] Elliot: That helps. For the tabletop we want to simulate a region-level KMS outage plus increased latencies. Can Redwood simulate load or will we need to run traffic from our side?
[00:18:55] Priya: We can spin up a controlled load test tied to your tenancy and coordinate throttle rules; we'll prepare a script you can run or we can run in collaboration.

[00:22:05] Jordan: On SLAs, what's the uptime SLA for Dedicated vs Private? And is there a credits model for breaches?
[00:22:14] Alex: Dedicated typically has a 99.9x SLA depending on the contract tier; Private (on-prem) has support SLAs and a runbook but uptime is managed by customer infrastructure. SLA credits are tiered — small percentage credits per minute/hour of downtime after thresholds. We'll share the standard SLA doc and adjust for your procurement.

[00:25:00] Lina: We need to understand monitoring thresholds that trigger executive notification — e.g., if checkout latency > X% for 5 minutes escalate to execs.
[00:25:10] Priya: We can map to percentiles: p95 latency increase, error rate > Y%, or sustained token failures. These thresholds are configurable and we can add a webhook to send to your PagerDuty escalation.

[00:28:30] Alex: A few clarifications from prior emails: data residency — you mentioned EU-only. We can ensure model weights and keys stay in EU regions for the tenant and disable cross-region replication for that tenancy.
[00:28:44] Elliot: Yes, all EU for payment data. Also, we'd prefer logs to remain in EU and be accessible under our retention policy.
[00:29:00] Priya: We'll set ingestion and storage to EU endpoints and enable object-lock policies per your retention spec.

[00:31:12] Sam: Contractually we'll ask for SOC 2 and a list of sub-processors. Please include a sub-processor list and any third-party auditors.
[00:31:22] Alex: We'll attach a current sub-processor list and last audit firm name.

[00:33:00] Jordan: For the BCDR tabletop, what are suggested scenarios?
[00:33:06] Priya: Typical scenarios: region outage, KMS provider outage, control plane partition, and data corruption event. Each scenario includes RTO/RPO targets, failover commands, and communication templates.
[00:33:30] Lina: For data corruption we need point-in-time recovery and a way to validate model integrity.
[00:33:38] Priya: We snapshot model checkpoints and keep signed artifact manifests; you can validate via signature to ensure no tampering.

[00:36:05] Alex: Let's recap next steps before we run out of time. I'll send the SOC2 Type II and the spreadsheet mapping; Priya will send KMS architecture and a redacted runbook; you (Elliot) will provide RTO/RPO per workload; Jordan to invite runbook owners to tabletop.
[00:36:24] Jordan: Sounds good. We'll also prepare a short list of priority routes (checkout, recommendations) for warm-pinning.
[00:36:35] Elliot: We'll aim to have RTO targets listed by 2026-05-12.

[00:40:10] Priya: One more practical item — during key rotation we recommend a two-phase roll: stage new key, re-encrypt metadata, then rotate. We'll include commands and a rollback path in the runbook.
[00:40:32] Sam: Legal will want the rollback criteria and proof of successful rotation logs.
[00:40:38] Alex: We'll add sample audit excerpts.

[00:46:20] Lina: Any major blockers? Cost will be a factor — pinned pools increase cost. We need a TCO estimate for keeping a pinned pool for checkout.
[00:46:30] Alex: We'll include a TCO worksheet with cost vs RTO tradeoffs. That's in scope for the next artifact.

[00:49:05] Priya: We'll also propose quantization/packing options to reduce memory and warm-up time if you want to trade some latency for cost.
[00:49:18] Elliot: Good to know.

[00:51:00] Alex: Thanks everyone. We'll circulate the artifacts and follow up with calendar for the tabletop.
[00:51:10] Lina: Thanks — appreciated.

End of transcript.
